channel.title: Bruce B. A. West / Field Notes
channel.description: Research and practice notes on AI systems, strategy, organizational transformation, knowledge infrastructure, and accountable innovation.

item.title: The CMMC suspension is an organizational knowledge test
item.description: The CMMC Phase II suspension lowers the immediate pressure of third-party certification, but it does not remove the obligation to protect defense data—or the need to preserve the organizational knowledge built around that work.

item.title: From signals to strategic options
item.description: How agentic AI can help turn scattered external change into evidence-backed innovation options without replacing strategic judgment.

item.title: Model the builders, not only the models
item.description: Why agent-based modeling could help explain how builder-side review networks, routing policies, and AI-mediated deliberation create—or erode—accountability before deployment.

item.title: Networked accountability: a working research direction
item.description: A working research direction for understanding how review networks determine which AI risks become visible, credible, and actionable.

item.title: From AI ambition to adopted capability
item.description: Why serious AI strategy must connect technical possibility to evidence, operating mechanisms, adoption, and accountable ownership.

item.title: Knowledge infrastructure is AI infrastructure
item.description: AI systems inherit the strengths and weaknesses of the organizational knowledge environments in which they are expected to operate.

item.title: AI is moving from answers into systems
item.description: As 2025 closes, faster frontier models matter less as isolated releases than as components in agents, tools, infrastructure, controls, and organizational work systems.

item.title: Open agent protocols need institutions
item.description: Donating MCP to a neutral foundation shows what agent interoperability needs beyond a specification: stewardship, legitimacy, compatibility, security response, and durable participation.

item.title: AI productivity can hide a learning debt
item.description: AI can help experienced workers move faster and cross functional boundaries, but organizations must watch for learning debt when automation removes the difficult practice through which expertise grows.

item.title: Multi-model cloud is a governance choice
item.description: Making another frontier model available through an established cloud platform reduces acquisition friction, but a durable multi-model strategy requires routing criteria, common evidence, and portability.

item.title: Human-like perception is not human judgment
item.description: Research aligning visual representations with human concepts can make AI more useful and robust, but perceptual agreement remains distinct from accountable human judgment.

item.title: Enterprise AI at 350,000 seats is an organizational redesign
item.description: A planned AI rollout to 350,000 employees is not a software deployment. It is a redesign of work, learning, controls, support, measurement, and professional identity.

item.title: A safety classifier is policy made executable
item.description: Open safety reasoning models make an important governance fact visible: a classifier operationalizes policy choices and therefore needs ownership, evaluation, appeals, and change control.

item.title: Shared AI workspaces need shared accountability
item.description: As AI gains access to company knowledge and desktop applications, shared context must be matched by ownership, provenance, permissions, and decision records.

item.title: AI infrastructure strategy is becoming full-stack strategy
item.description: October announcements spanning fusion control and custom accelerators show AI strategy extending through models, software, networks, chips, energy, and physical systems.

item.title: Visual agent builders do not remove engineering
item.description: Visual agent builders make orchestration more accessible and legible, but production systems still require architecture, evaluation, security, versioning, and operational ownership.

item.title: Long-horizon agents need short feedback loops
item.description: Models that sustain work for hours make checkpointing, observability, bounded authority, and inexpensive reversal more important—not less.

item.title: At the edge, every joule is a model requirement
item.description: DARPA's energy-aware machine-learning program makes an essential systems point: at the tactical edge, performance per joule belongs in the model requirement from the beginning.

item.title: Coding agents need a new definition of done
item.description: Longer-running coding agents can finish larger tasks, but engineering teams need a definition of done that includes evidence, reviewability, security, operability, and team learning.

item.title: When AI creates the file, provenance becomes part of the deliverable
item.description: As AI systems create spreadsheets, documents, presentations, and reports, organizations must treat provenance, review, and reproducibility as part of the finished product.

item.title: AI earns trust in critical systems through control
item.description: Deep Loop Shaping at LIGO illustrates how AI enters a critical system: inside bounded feedback loops, against physical measures, with simulation, hardware testing, and continuing human control.

item.title: Agentic cyber threats collapse the distance between intent and action
item.description: Agentic cyber misuse compresses planning, coding, adaptation, and execution. Defenders need equally integrated sensing, decision, and response loops without automating away judgment.

item.title: Reorganization will not substitute for an adoption system

item.title: AI security overlays can connect two professions

item.title: The AI Cyber Challenge makes evaluation operational

item.title: The federal AI inventory is becoming an operating instrument

Identifying human contributions in AI-assisted inventions can be challenging, as there is no definitive test. However, the USPTO’s guidelines lay out several integral principles to aid in this process. It notes that a person’s utilization of AI in the invention process does not disqualify them as an inventor, but simply presenting a problem to an AI system might not suffice for inventorship. With its new guidance, USPTO navigates the intricate landscape of human inventorship in the age of AI, offering a more unambiguous path to patentability. The agency will now seek public comments on the guidance over the next three months.
